sections.title: The Americas: Caribbean and Afro-Latin Education Studies
sections.description: This course surveys the histories and social worlds of Africans and their descendants across North, South, and Latin America, including Afro‑Latins and other African‑diasporic communities, while foregrounding education, artistic expression, religion, and spirituality. The curriculum highlights how geography, history, culture, race, and ethnicity have shaped distinctive educational challenges and opportunities, underscoring the arts and spiritual traditions as significant forms of informal education, community resilience, and resistance. The course begins by exploring the experiences of Africans and their descendants in the southern United States during and after the antebellum and Spanish colonial periods, emphasizing ethnic and racial formations and contributions to cultural development. It then considers the interconnected relationships among learning, cultural expression, religion, spirituality, and community-building across the U.S. South, the Caribbean, and Afro-Latin America. The course pays particular attention to migration narratives and how these communities have navigated and resisted educational oppression in the U.S., Latin America and the Caribbean, creating their own learning and cultural spaces. Participants will engage deeply with oral history, primary and secondary sources, including historical documents, literature from writers such as Zora Neale Hurston and José Martí, documentaries, scholarly articles, music, visual art, and performance. Students will conduct original research at the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture and travel to Harlem, New York, as part of a class field trip.
